titles.l1: Four ways to be right or wrong

kernelIdea: Prove ∀ by arguing about an arbitrary element; disprove ∀ with one counterexample. Prove ∃ by exhibiting a witness; disprove ∃ by proving the universal negation. Prove ∃! by exhibiting and then showing any two candidates coincide.

kernels.l1: There are two ways to be right and two ways to be wrong. Which one you need depends on the first word.
kernels.l2: To show an every telling is true, give a reason that works for any one of them. To show it is false, find one bad apple. To show a some telling is true, find one. To show it is false, check them all.
kernels.l3: To prove a for all claim, take any one and follow it: argue about a case you know nothing special about. To disprove it, give one counterexample. To prove a there exists claim, show one example. To disprove it, argue that every case fails.
kernels.l4: Prove a *for all* claim by taking one unnamed member and following it; disprove it with a single case that fails. Prove a *there exists* claim by exhibiting one that works.
kernels.l5: Each of the four proof tasks has its own template: an unnamed member, a single failing case, one worked example, and ruling out every candidate — plus the two-part pattern for uniqueness.
kernels.l6: The strategy for a quantified goal is decided by the outermost quantifier and by whether you are proving or refuting; splitting into cases is legitimate exactly when the cases cover everything.
kernels.l7: The four tasks — proving and disproving each of the two quantifiers — have fixed templates determined by the negation laws. The *for all* proof rests on naming one unnamed member and using nothing special about it.
kernels.l8: Universal generalization is sound exactly because the element chosen is arbitrary but fixed — free of any hypothesis particular to it; existential instantiation dually introduces a fresh constant, and confusing the two is the standard source of fallacious quantifier reasoning.
